newsitem.title: USA: Natl Semiconductor has sharp loss.
newsitem.headline: Natl Semiconductor has sharp loss.

text.p: National Semiconductor Corp., one of the nation's largest makers of semiconductors, reported a sharp loss Thursday for its fiscal first quarter after charges of $285.6 million for spinning off a unit.
However, in a sign of a possible upturn for the beleaguered microchip industry, new product orders actually improved during the quarter, the company said.

National Semiconductor reported a net loss of $207.6 million, or $1.51 a share, on revenues of $566.1 million for its first quarter ended Aug. 25. The results compared with a profit of $73.5 million, or 53 cents a share, on sales of $698.8 million last year.
Excluding the charges, the company would have reported a first-quarter net profit of $6.5 million, or 5 cents a share.
Shares of the chipmaker lost 62.5 cents to $17.125 on the New York Stock Exchange.
In June, National Semiconductor said it would spin its logic, memory and discrete microchip products into a new company, Fairchild Semiconductor.

Although worldwide chip orders were down 10 percent from the first quarter a year ago, they actually grew from fourth-quarter levels at a percentage rate in the mid-teens and proved strongest toward the final few weeks of the quarter.
"Bookings showed improvement throughout the quarter, but we will maintain guarded optimism for a while longer before declaring a trend," said Chief Executive Brian Halla.
Semiconductor makers have been plagued throughout 1996 by slower orders as end users, such as personal computer and other electronic equipment makers, have reduced inventories.
National Semiconductor said PC makers showed the strongest growth rate in orders in the first quarter, due to demand for Pentium-compatible chips, which nearly doubled from the fourth quarter.

Chip orders for local area networks and wireless communications products also continue to grow while analogue multi-market and logic multi-market orders -- though up in the quarter's final few weeks -- fell from last year's rates.
The company said orders in North America and Southeast Asia were up from spring months, though orders in Europe and Japan were flat.
